sentences.text: Benefits verification for A-B-A therapy isn't one answer.
Each case covers eight C-P-T codes, and each code has its own copay, auth rule, session limit and place of service.
That's sixty-eight scored fields per case.
Grade the whole case right or wrong, and you can't see which field broke.
Here, version one gets ninety-seven percent of fields right, but only twenty-two percent of cases.
So this prototype scores every field, and sends only the risky cases to a person.
On the write side, a seeded generator makes two hundred forty synthetic cases from four fictional payers.
An extractor reads each one with two prompt versions, and stores typed results in S-Q-Lite.
On the read side, validation, routing and scoring run when a page loads, cached until a gold label changes.
Only the extractor could be a model, through an optional Lite L-L-M path.
Everything else is plain, deterministic Python.

scenes.title: Trace, part 1: one case becomes a typed result

sentences.text: Let's follow one case.
The generator writes a portal-style document with noise, like a copay spelled out in words, and records where each value sits.
Then, extract mock runs with prompt version two.
It returns a V-O-B Result, where every field carries a value, a confidence from zero to one, and the source span it came from.

scenes.title: Trace, part 2: rules, routing and the review queue

sentences.text: Next, validate runs twelve rules against a per-payer table.
Deductible met can't exceed the deductible.
Auth must match the payer's rule for that code.
Then, route decides.
If any field is under the threshold, zero point eight by default, or any rule fails, the case goes to review.
Otherwise, it's auto-approved.
Flagged cases sort by risk.
At zero point eight, version one auto-approves thirty-two percent of cases, and escaped errors fall from seventy-seven percent of cases to thirteen.

scenes.title: Trace, part 3: the reviewer closes the loop

sentences.text: On the case page, source spans glow red for a failed rule, and amber for low confidence.
The reviewer fixes a value, and saves it as gold.
That write is append-only: a new row tagged human, with a timestamp, and the latest row wins.
The gold revision changes, so the cached snapshot rebuilds, and accuracy recomputes.
Scoring is exact match after normalization, so twenty-five dollars and twenty-five point zero zero are equal.
For A/B, a seeded hash of the case I-D splits cases fifty-fifty.
The bootstrap resamples whole cases, because fields within a case are correlated.
Version two fixes session limits and place of service.
But copay drops thirty-nine points for one payer, Northwind.
Averaged across payers, that looks modest.
Any significant regression means hold.
To run it, type make demo.
It generates the data, runs both versions, and serves the UI on port eight thousand, with no A-P-I keys.
Now, some gotchas.
The mock extractor isn't a model.
It starts from the gold labels and injects seeded errors, so its numbers say nothing about a real system.
Make demo wipes reviewer labels.
Human labels get no second review.
And escaped errors are counted against all cases, not just auto-approved ones.
To recap.
Score fields, not cases.
Route on confidence and rules.
Reviewer fixes become gold.
Compare prompts per payer, so regressions can't hide in averages.
Next steps: calibrated thresholds per field, weighting errors by billing impact, double review of human labels, and the same eval on real, de-identified model output.
Thank you for watching.
